title: Linux 7.3 Improves Performance When Running Out of VRAM
summary: The article details technical improvements in Linux 7.3 for managing VRAM overcommitment, focusing on performance and stability when applications exceed available VRAM. Key enhancements include fixing kernel deadlock issues during memory eviction, reducing unnecessary memory transfers between VRAM and CPU RAM, and addressing physical memory fragmentation for display scanout buffers. These changes aim to minimize performance degradation and crashes when VRAM is overcommitted.
key_points: VRAM overcommitment is theoretically a performance issue, not a stability one, but practical implementations often lead to crashes or severe slowdowns.
Accessing CPU RAM from the GPU is significantly slower due to PCIe latency and bandwidth limitations, with PCIe 4.0x16 offering ~32GiB/s bandwidth.
Cache behavior plays a critical role in mitigating performance penalties when VRAM is overcommitted, as cached data avoids PCIe latency.
Linux 7.3 addresses kernel deadlocks during command submission by implementing proper deadlock detection and retry mechanisms using `drm_exec`.
Memory eviction in VRAM can lead to 'ping-pong' effects, where allocations are constantly moved between VRAM and CPU RAM, degrading performance.
Display scanout buffers require physically contiguous VRAM, leading to excessive evictions when VRAM is fragmented, sometimes evicting up to 4GiB of data for a ~32MiB buffer.
The article highlights ongoing work to optimize VRAM management, including better heuristics for memory eviction and allocation.
